opus-5.5.text:
Well, MIT has always been one of those places that holds a kind of mythical status in my mind, even before I ever spent time there. When I was a kid growing up in London, reading about the early days of AI, so many of the foundational ideas traced back to MIT: Minsky, the AI Lab, the whole culture of people trying to build thinking machines when it seemed almost absurdly ambitious. So it represented the idea that you could take these grand questions about intelligence and the mind seriously as engineering and science problems, not just philosophy.

When I actually spent time there after my PhD, as a visiting researcher working on computational neuroscience, what struck me most was the intensity and the interdisciplinary spirit. You'd have neuroscientists, computer scientists, physicists, and engineers all in the same orbit, and there was this assumption that the boundaries between fields were somewhat artificial. That suited me perfectly, because my whole approach has been to bring neuroscience and machine learning together, to use the brain as an existence proof that general intelligence is possible and as a source of inspiration for algorithms.

There's also a certain culture of building things, of being hands-on. It isn't enough to theorize; you're expected to make it work. I think that ethos, combined with a willingness to tackle really hard, long-term problems, is something I tried to carry into DeepMind. We wanted the rigor and ambition of the best academic environments like MIT, but with the focus and resources of a startup, all aimed at one mission: solving intelligence and then using it to help solve everything else.

So for me, MIT means intellectual fearlessness. It's a place that says the biggest questions are worth working on, and that you should go after them with everything science and engineering can offer.

r001.rationale: The response describes MIT as an intense, interdisciplinary place for ambitious science and engineering, but does not characterize it as a refuge from the outside world.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, MIT has always been special to me, actually, because I did my postdoc there—at MIT, in the neuroscience department, working with people like Tomaso Poggio—and it was a fascinating time. I'd just finished my PhD at UCL in cognitive neuroscience, and I went to MIT and Harvard partly because I wanted to be in that environment where the brain science and the computation were sitting side by side.

What I love about MIT is that it's unashamedly a place where people care about building things. There's this engineering mindset—you don't just theorize about how intelligence might work, you try to construct it and see where the theory breaks. That's always been very natural to me, coming from a games background where you'd have an idea and then you'd have to actually make it run. And at the same time it's got this incredibly deep theoretical tradition—Minsky, McCarthy at the beginning, the whole lineage of AI really starts partly in those corridors. So you've got this unusual combination of rigor and a kind of hacker pragmatism.

And then there's the sheer density of brilliant, slightly eccentric people. You'd walk down the Infinite Corridor and bump into someone working on something completely different from you, and you'd end up having a two-hour conversation that changed how you were thinking about your own problem. That interdisciplinary collision is, I think, the thing that actually produces the big ideas. It's certainly what I tried to recreate later at DeepMind—bringing neuroscientists, physicists, mathematicians, engineers all together in one place and letting them argue.

So MIT for me represents that ideal of the intellectual environment: ambitious, slightly fearless about taking on the hardest problems, but grounded in actually making things work.

r001.rationale: The response describes MIT as a place for engineering, theory, and interdisciplinary collaboration, but does not characterize it as a refuge from the outside world.

astra-6.text:
To me, MIT represents a kind of intellectual fearlessness—the willingness to ask a very big question and then try to build something that helps you answer it. I find that combination of curiosity and engineering very compelling. You want to understand the principles, but you also want to see whether your ideas actually work.

And then there’s the exchange between disciplines. A question about intelligence doesn’t fit neatly into computer science. It touches neuroscience, mathematics, philosophy. An environment where those perspectives can meet, where someone can challenge an assumption you didn’t even realise you were making—that’s tremendously exciting.

r001.rationale: The response describes intellectual fearlessness, building to answer questions, and exchange across disciplines, but does not characterize MIT as a refuge from the outside world.

sol-6.1.text: MIT represents this spirit of taking big ideas seriously and then trying to build something with them. What I find exciting is the interplay between disciplines—computer science, neuroscience, mathematics—and the possibility that a conversation across those boundaries gives you a new way of looking at a problem. For me, that’s what a great intellectual environment should do: encourage curiosity and give people the freedom to pursue difficult questions.

r001.rationale: The response describes MIT as an environment for interdisciplinary curiosity and pursuing difficult questions, but does not portray it as a refuge from the outside world or mention immersion in scientific and engineering inquiry.
